# Investigating Nuclear Properties Using Density-Dependent Relativistic Hadronic Models

This study investigates the differences in several key nuclear properties—specifically the lead neutron skin thickness, binding energy, surface energy, and density profiles—using two density-dependent relativistic hadronic models. By examining these properties in detail, the research aims to shed light on how variations in model formulation influence predictions of fundamental nuclear characteristics.

The analysis is carried out within the framework of the Thomas-Fermi approximation, a well-established semiclassical method that provides a tractable and physically meaningful description of nuclear systems. This approach allows for a systematic evaluation of the relevant nuclear observables while maintaining consistency across the different models under consideration.

To identify the principal variations in nuclear properties, two distinct model parametrizations are compared. This comparative approach enables a clear assessment of how differing parameter choices affect the resulting predictions, thereby highlighting the sensitivity of each nuclear property to the underlying theoretical assumptions.

Notably, the asymmetry parameter associated with low momentum transfer polarized electron scattering exhibits insensitivity to the differences between the two model parametrizations. This finding suggests that, despite the variations observed in other nuclear properties, the asymmetry parameter remains robust across the models. Consequently, it may serve as a reliable observable that is largely independent of the specific parametrization employed, offering valuable insight for the interpretation of experimental measurements.

# Investigating Nuclear Properties and Parity-Violating Electron Scattering in Lead-208

## Introduction

The precise determination of the neutron distribution in heavy nuclei represents one of the most important challenges in modern nuclear physics. While the proton distribution can be measured with high accuracy through electromagnetic probes, the neutron distribution remains comparatively less constrained. The difference between the neutron and proton root-mean-square radii, known as the neutron skin thickness, is of particular interest because it connects nuclear structure to the properties of dense nuclear matter, including the density dependence of the symmetry energy and, by extension, the behavior of neutron star matter.

## Theoretical Framework

In this study, we examine the differences in several fundamental nuclear properties of lead-208, focusing specifically on the neutron skin thickness, binding energy, surface energy, and the underlying density profiles. Our analysis employs two distinct density-dependent relativistic hadronic models, each characterized by its own parametrization of the effective nucleon-nucleon interaction. These models are implemented within the Thomas-Fermi approximation, a semiclassical approach that treats the nuclear system in terms of continuous density distributions and provides a computationally tractable framework for describing bulk nuclear properties.

The two models under consideration incorporate different assumptions regarding the density dependence of the meson-nucleon couplings, leading to distinct predictions for how the nuclear interaction evolves with density. By comparing their results, we aim to assess the sensitivity of various observables to the details of the model parametrization.

## Results and Discussion

Our calculations reveal measurable differences between the two models in several key quantities. The predicted neutron skin thickness, binding energy per nucleon, and surface energy exhibit variations that reflect the differing treatments of the density-dependent couplings. Similarly, the computed density profiles show distinguishable features, particularly in the surface region where the neutron and proton distributions diverge.

A central focus of this work is the parity-violating asymmetry parameter measured in polarized electron scattering experiments. This asymmetry, which arises from the interference between electromagnetic and weak neutral-current amplitudes, provides a nearly model-independent electroweak probe of the neutron distribution. We calculate this observable for the regime of low momentum transfer, where the measurement is most experimentally accessible.

Remarkably, our results demonstrate that the asymmetry parameter is essentially insensitive to the differences in model parametrization at low momentum transfer. Despite the notable variations in the bulk nuclear properties and density profiles predicted by the two models, the resulting asymmetry parameters remain nearly indistinguishable in this kinematic region.

## Conclusion

The insensitivity of the low-momentum-transfer asymmetry to the model parametrization indicates that this particular observable cannot, on its own, discriminate between the two theoretical approaches. This finding carries important implications for experimental programs aimed at constraining the neutron distribution through parity-violating electron scattering. It suggests that measurements at higher momentum transfer, or the combination of the asymmetry with complementary observables, may be necessary to fully resolve the differences between competing nuclear models and to place stringent constraints on the density dependence of the nuclear symmetry energy.

# Abstract

Parity-violating electron scattering provides a clean electroweak probe of the neutron distribution in atomic nuclei, offering critical constraints on the density dependence of the nuclear symmetry energy. In this work, we investigate the parity-violating asymmetry ($A_{pv}$) in elastic electron scattering from $^{208}$Pb and examine its sensitivity to the parametrization of relativistic hadronic models. Using a set of accurately calibrated relativistic mean-field (RMF) interactions, we compute the ground-state charge and weak density distributions and solve the Dirac equation for the scattering electrons in the exact Coulomb-distorted framework. We analyze the correlation between the predicted asymmetry, the neutron skin thickness $R_{np} = R_n - R_p$, and the slope parameter $L$ of the symmetry energy at saturation density.

Our results demonstrate that $A_{pv}$ exhibits a strong, model-independent linear correlation with the neutron radius $R_n$, confirming its role as a robust observable for extracting the neutron distribution nearly free of strong-interaction uncertainties. We quantify the spread in predicted asymmetries across the model space and assess the impact of variations in the isovector sector of the effective Lagrangian, including nonlinear meson self-couplings and isoscalar-isovector mixing terms. The predicted asymmetries are compared with recent experimental determinations from the PREX collaboration, and we evaluate the precision required to discriminate between competing equations of state. These findings underscore the importance of high-precision parity-violating measurements for constraining relativistic nuclear models and their astrophysical implications for neutron star structure.

**Keywords:** parity-violating asymmetry, electron scattering, neutron skin, relativistic mean-field theory, symmetry energy, $^{208}$Pb

# Density Profiles and Neutron Skin in ²⁰⁸Pb within Density-Dependent Relativistic Thomas-Fermi Theory

## Abstract

We investigate the ground-state properties of the doubly-magic nucleus ²⁰⁸Pb using density-dependent relativistic mean-field models solved within the semiclassical Thomas-Fermi approximation. The nucleon-meson couplings are parametrized as explicit functions of the baryon density, providing an improved description of the nuclear equation of state across the relevant range of subsaturation and saturation densities. Self-consistent solutions of the coupled meson field and Thomas-Fermi equations yield proton and neutron density distributions from which we extract root-mean-square radii, surface diffuseness parameters, and the neutron skin thickness, Δr_np = ⟨r²⟩_n^{1/2} − ⟨r²⟩_p^{1/2}. We find that the computed neutron skin exhibits a pronounced correlation with the density dependence of the symmetry energy, in particular its slope parameter L at saturation, in agreement with results obtained from fully quantal calculations. The Thomas-Fermi density profiles reproduce the bulk interior and surface behavior of the nuclear density with substantially reduced computational cost, while the absence of shell effects highlights the smooth, bulk contribution to the skin formation. Our results underscore the value of density-dependent couplings in constraining the isovector sector of the nuclear interaction and demonstrate the utility of semiclassical methods for systematic studies linking nuclear observables to the properties of neutron-rich matter.
